name: React Native

foundation.via: Contributed by Meta together with React

summary: React for Android and iOS apps: JavaScript runs in the Hermes engine inside the app, and React components become real platform views, with JavaScript and native code calling each other directly through JSI.
intro: A React Native app is a native app with a JavaScript engine inside it. You write React components with core primitives such as `View`, `Text` and `Image`, and the renderer, Fabric, turns them into the platform’s own views on Android and iOS, so buttons, text input and scrolling behave like any other app’s. JavaScript runs in Hermes, an engine built for React Native that compiles release builds to bytecode ahead of time; Hermes V1 has been the default since 0.84 (February 2026). Since the New Architecture became the default in 0.76 (October 2024), JavaScript and native code talk through JSI, a C++ interface that lets JavaScript hold references to native objects and call their methods directly, instead of the old asynchronous bridge that serialized every message. Device features come from Turbo Native Modules written in Kotlin, Java, Swift, Objective-C or C++, and during development the Metro bundler serves your JavaScript with Fast Refresh.

The project releases a new minor version about every two months and supports the latest three; it is still numbered 0.x. React Native 0.82 (October 2025) was the first that runs only on the New Architecture, and 0.84 stopped including legacy code in iOS builds. 0.88 (October 2026) ships React 19.3, makes web-style event dispatching the default and adds variable fonts and iOS SceneDelegate support, with no user-facing breaking changes. The docs recommend starting with a framework, naming Expo, rather than the bare template. Beyond phones, React Native runs on Meta Quest headsets, and other teams maintain out-of-tree platforms such as Windows and macOS. Meta built it and contributed it to the React Foundation on February 24, 2026.
strengths: Real platform views instead of a web page, so apps get native scrolling, text input and accessibility
One React codebase and one set of skills for Android, iOS and the web, with npm packages and React libraries shared between them
Fast Refresh shows JavaScript edits in the running app without rebuilding the native binary
New Architecture features: synchronous layout measurement, concurrent React (Transitions, Suspense) and direct JavaScript-to-native calls through JSI
limits: Still 0.x, with a minor release about every two months and only the latest three supported, so apps have to keep upgrading; some releases still contain breaking changes
Native work doesn’t go away: device features without a library need a module in Kotlin or Swift, and building still needs Xcode and Android Studio unless a service such as EAS Build does it
Libraries that only supported the old bridge no longer work since 0.82, when the Legacy Architecture could no longer be enabled
The New Architecture doesn’t make an app faster by itself; the docs say apps may need refactoring to use synchronous layout or concurrent features

snippet.title: A new app without a framework: start Metro, then build and run on a device
source: npx @react-native-community/cli@latest init MyApp   # bare template: android/, ios/ and App.tsx
npx react-native start                               # Metro serves the JavaScript with Fast Refresh
npx react-native run-android                         # build the Android app, install it on an emulator or device
cd ios && bundle exec pod install && cd ..          # CocoaPods for the iOS project
npx react-native run-ios                             # build and launch in the iOS Simulator
# the docs' recommended start instead: React Native with the Expo framework

sections.title: Legacy and New Architecture
sections.intro: The New Architecture replaced how JavaScript reaches native code. Apps and libraries had to move between 0.76, when it became the default, and 0.82, when the old path was switched off.

rows.label: JavaScript ↔ native
values: An asynchronous bridge that serialized every message
JSI: JavaScript holds references to C++ objects and calls them directly

rows.label: Rendering
values: The original renderer; layout read back asynchronously, so `onLayout` updates could paint a frame late
Fabric, with synchronous layout access and support for concurrent React

rows.label: Native modules
values: Native Modules called over the bridge
Turbo Native Modules called through JSI

rows.label: Status
values: Frozen in 0.80; ignored from 0.82; removed from iOS builds in 0.84
Default since 0.76 (October 2024); the only option since 0.82

story: Facebook first showed React Native in early 2015 as a way to bring React’s model to mobile, open-sourced it for iOS in March 2015 and added Android in September, when it described its first cross-platform React Native app, Ads Manager. The idea was to render real platform views from JavaScript rather than a web page in a WebView.

As apps grew, the asynchronous bridge became a bottleneck, and Meta spent years on a rewrite. Hermes became the default engine in 0.70 (September 2022), and the New Architecture, with JSI, the Fabric renderer and Turbo Native Modules, became the default in 0.76 (October 2024). 0.82 (October 2025) made it the only architecture, and 0.84 (February 2026) made Hermes V1 the default.

Meta announced in October 2025 that React Native would move to the React Foundation with React. The move took effect on February 24, 2026, the same day React Native came to Meta Quest, and its repository moved to the `react` GitHub organisation in June. 0.88 followed in October 2026.

choices.choice: Native views instead of a WebView
choices.why: Rendering the platform’s own controls gives apps native look, feel and accessibility, at the cost of keeping a native layer per platform.

Serializing every call across an asynchronous bridge made frequent updates and large data, such as camera frames, slow; direct references to C++ objects remove the copying and allow synchronous calls.
Hermes compiles JavaScript to bytecode during the build, which the docs say improves start-up time and cuts memory use and app size compared with JavaScriptCore.

choices.choice: Point new users to a framework
choices.why: Routing, native builds and upgrades are hard to get right in a bare app, so the docs now recommend starting with a framework such as Expo.

timeline.text: Open-sourced for iOS in March; Android support in September
Hermes becomes the default engine in 0.70
The New Architecture becomes the default in 0.76
0.82 runs only on the New Architecture
Hermes V1 default in 0.84; moves to the React Foundation on February 24; 0.88 in October
